analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student aid to colleges whose programs leave students unable to qualify for required licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it drew no cosponsors in either party.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut off federal student aid — including Pell Grants, workforce funding, GI Bill benefits, and military tuition assistance — to college programs that prepare students for licensed professions (nursing, cosmetology, trucking, and similar fields) unless the program actually qualifies graduates to sit for the required license exam in the states where they live or where the school recruits. It would also require schools to arrange clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships, to certify that their vocational programs meet accreditation and licensure prerequisites, to make students sign a written acknowledgment if a program does not meet a state's licensure requirements, and to be legally authorized in every state where it enrolls online students.
analysis.who_benefits: Students who borrow or use GI Bill and workforce dollars to pay for programs meant to lead to a licensed job. Today a school can enroll a student in an online program, take the federal aid, and leave the graduate unable to qualify for the exam in their own state; the bill would make federal aid conditional on the program actually qualifying students for licensure where the school recruits or operates. Students considering programs that fall short would at least get a written warning and would have to acknowledge it by hand before enrolling.

how_it_helps.text: Makes a school ineligible for federal financial assistance for any program leading to a licensed occupation unless completing the program fully qualifies a student to take the required exam and be licensed in the student's state and in any state the school advertises or recruits in [S2][S3].
Requires the school to provide timely placement for academically required pre-licensure steps such as clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships [S2][S3].

Requires schools to certify that their gainful employment programs are accredited and meet state licensure prerequisites, and to obtain a signed, handwritten statement from a student before enrolling them in a program that does not meet the licensure requirements of the state where the student wants to work [S2][S3].

Requires distance-education and correspondence schools to be legally authorized in every state where their enrolled students live, with state complaint processes, while preserving existing multi-state reciprocity agreements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: College programs — disproportionately for-profit and online career schools — whose degrees or certificates do not qualify graduates for the licenses they advertise for. Those programs would lose access to federal aid dollars or have to rework their programs to satisfy state licensure requirements and arrange clinical placements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Career programs that fail licensure rules

drawbacks.text: The acknowledgment requirement still lets a school enroll a student in a program that does not meet the state's licensure requirements, so long as the student signs a statement saying they wish to enroll anyway [S3].

Requiring programs to qualify graduates for licensure in the student's home metro area and in every state a school advertises in is a demanding standard for institutions operating across many states, and could push some schools to restrict enrollment to fewer states or exit licensed fields altogether [S3].
Compliance and certification costs fall on schools, including legitimate programs that would have to document licensure prerequisites for each state they serve [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — no federal aid for programs that leave graduates ineligible for the license exam the program advertises toward — addresses a real and costly failure for students who borrow for worthless credentials. The bill is blunt, and the handwritten-acknowledgment escape hatch means some students could still be enrolled into noncompliant programs. But the acknowledgment at least forces disclosure before the student spends years and federal aid dollars.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, sent to a subcommittee a month later, and then sat with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on November 21, 2019 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Education and Labor Committee and also to Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs for the portions within their jurisdiction [S5].
On December 19, 2019, it was referred to the Economic Opportunity Subcommittee of Veterans' Affairs, and no further action of any kind was taken for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: College programs whose credentials do not qualify graduates for the licenses they advertise kept full access to federal student aid, GI Bill dollars, and workforce funding, and faced no new licensure, placement, or disclosure requirements. Students remained exposed to borrowing for programs that do not lead to the advertised license.

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three House committees; no colleague signed on as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote over the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Veterans' Affairs and Armed Services Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after the December 2019 subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor votes were ever held and the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan breakdown of support exists.

industries.note: These schools rely on federal student aid for much of their revenue and include the programs most likely to fail the bill's test — online degrees in licensed fields that do not qualify graduates for licensure exams in the states where students live. The bill would cut off federal aid to those programs or force them to rework curricula and arrange clinical placements, which cuts directly into enrollment they profit from.

industries.industry: Accrediting agencies and state licensing bodies
industries.note: Schools would have to document programmatic accreditation and state licensure prerequisites in every state they serve, adding compliance burden but pointing to the accreditation and licensing system schools already claim to meet. No new power is created; the bill simply makes aid eligibility depend on it.

industries.industry: Distance-education providers and state reciprocity agreements
industries.note: The bill would codify the requirement that online schools be authorized in each state where students live, while continuing to recognize multi-state reciprocity agreements. Online programs keep the reciprocity pathway but must document that each state has a working complaint process.
